description: Curated headlines about data center water use, regulation, enforcement, and solutions — linked to the tracker's datasets where possible.

items.title: ITIF Report: Data Center Water Problem Is 'Soluble' But Needs Coordinated State Policy
items.summary: An ITIF report by Robin Gaster argues data centers directly consumed ~17.4 billion gallons for cooling in 2023 versus ~211 billion gallons indirectly through electricity generation (about 12x more), and that water stress is regional (Pacific Northwest power generation uses 2.1 gal/kWh vs. 0.13 gal/kWh in solar-heavy California) rather than a uniform national problem. It recommends mandatory standardized water-use disclosure, watershed-based performance standards instead of technology mandates, integrated water-energy agency review, and a federal role limited to metrics/R&D/procurement rather than preempting state water law.

items.title: Nearly One-Third of Indiana Counties Now Restrict Data Centers
items.summary: An Indiana University Environmental Resilience Institute tally found 11 Indiana counties have passed data-center zoning ordinances, at least 17 have enacted temporary moratoriums, and two (Marshall and Cass counties) have full bans — making Indiana one of the most restricted states for new data-center siting. Cited drivers include water, electricity, land, noise, and air-quality concerns; the Indianapolis Metropolitan Development Commission separately voted 5-3 to recommend new zoning rules, and Meta's $10 billion Lebanon, IN project and a contested Martinsville-Brightwood project were cited as flashpoints.

items.title: Spartanburg County, SC Freezes Data-Center Applications for One Year Amid Water/Air Permit Fight
items.summary: Spartanburg County Council unanimously passed first reading of a 12-month data-center application moratorium on June 22, 2026, invoking the 'pending ordinance doctrine' to immediately freeze new applications — including a proposed Lighthouse Data Centers/Wharton Digital project at 300 Jones Road. The vote came days before SC DES held a June 25 public hearing on air and water discharge permits and increased power demand for the separate, already-under-construction Valara Holdings data center at the former Kohler plant site, which is exempt from the new moratorium. Part of a broader wave: several other SC counties have enacted or begun similar pauses in the absence of statewide rules.

items.title: Amazon Discloses First-Ever Global Data Center Water Use Figure: 2.5 Billion Gallons in 2025
items.summary: Amazon disclosed for the first time that its global data centers used 2.5 billion gallons of water in 2025, reporting a water usage effectiveness of 0.03 gallons/kWh — a 52% efficiency improvement since 2021 — and claiming it returned roughly two-thirds of that water to communities through infrastructure investment. AWS says its total water withdrawal decreased from 2024 to 2025 even as data center capacity expanded, a reversal of the industry-wide trend; the disclosure puts Amazon alongside Google, Meta, and Microsoft in publishing aggregate water figures (though still only company-wide totals, not facility-level).
items.cross_ref_note: Substantiates the existing wue-reporting solution entry in the Solutions tab

items.title: New York's Passed Data Center Bill Is a One-Year DEC Permit Moratorium, Not Just a SEQRA Trigger
items.summary: Legal analysis of the Responsible Data Center Development Act (A11560/S10642), passed by the legislature in early June and awaiting Gov. Hochul's signature, clarifies the bill imposes a one-year moratorium on new DEC permits/approvals for data centers of 20+ MW (exempting projects that have already started construction) — a stronger mechanism than a SEQRA environmental-review trigger alone. It requires water- and wastewater-impact disclosure at mandatory public hearings, a statewide environmental review of water use/discharge/thermal impacts, utility cost-recovery rules so data centers (not ratepayers) bear water-infrastructure upgrade costs, and host-community benefit programs addressing water impacts and cooling technology.
items.cross_ref_note: Clarifies the mechanism for NY S10642/A11560 in the Legislation tab is a DEC permit moratorium, not only a SEQRA review trigger

items.title: Missed Water Meter Let Georgia QTS Data Center Rack Up $147,000 Unbilled Bill
items.summary: A water meter serving Quality Technology Services' (QTS, owned by Blackstone) 615-acre 'Project Excalibur' data center campus in Fayetteville, Fayette County, GA was missed during the county's transition to smart advanced metering infrastructure, leaving roughly 13-15 million gallons of usage over six months uncaptured until residents in a nearby subdivision reported falling water pressure. Fayette County billed QTS about $147,000 retroactively (no fine was imposed), and county officials characterized it as an administrative oversight during the meter-system changeover rather than unauthorized water use.
items.cross_ref_note: Same incident tracked in Water Cases: QTS-Fayette-GA-unbilled-water-2026

items.title: Florida's Data Center Ratepayer and Reclaimed-Water Law Takes Effect
items.outlet: Data Center Dynamics / Fla. Governor's Office
items.summary: FL SB 484 — signed by Gov. DeSantis in May, bars utilities from passing data-center electricity costs onto residential ratepayers, requires 50+ MW users to pay full cost of service, and mandates reclaimed water for cooling at facilities using 100,000+ gallons/day where feasible — took effect July 1, 2026. Local governments keep zoning/denial authority, and the law tightens aquifer withdrawal permitting.
items.cross_ref_note: Full bill entry in Legislation tab: FL SB 484

items.title: Data Center Developer Who Vowed to Skip the Colorado River Now Sues For It
items.summary: Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing, which spent months publicly pledging its planned Imperial County AI complex would not touch a drop of Colorado River water, is now suing the Imperial Irrigation District for 260 million gallons/year after IID rejected its water application and cities' negotiations broke down. The developer argues fallowing 160 leased acres of farmland offsets the ~750,000 gal/day cooling demand, and challenges IID's tiered pricing (industrial rates up to ~$1,100/acre-foot vs. ~$20/acre-foot for agricultural use) as an unlawful barrier.
items.cross_ref_note: Related to the Imperial County moratorium fight already tracked: Imperial County, CA Declares Emergency Data-Center Moratorium; Developer Sues

items.title: Proposed Data Center Would Draw From Lake Supplying Most of Fort Worth's Drinking Water
items.summary: Kansas-based Diode Ventures has proposed a Henderson County data center that could draw up to 5 million gallons/day from Cedar Creek Lake, the reservoir supplying most of Fort Worth's drinking water, as area residents are asked to conserve amid drought-driven moderate water shortages. The West Cedar Creek Municipal Utility District had already advanced a temporary suspension of new 'high-intensity water service commitments' through April 1, 2027; the project's site review remains in early stages.

items.title: Jefferson County, PA Borough Passes 180-Day Data-Center Moratorium Over Water Supply
items.summary: Brookville Borough Council unanimously passed a 180-day moratorium on new data-center development and barred projects from drawing on borough water, after two prospective developments in nearby Pine Creek and Rose townships surfaced that could together use roughly 2.4 million gallons/day. The council says it isn't opposed to data centers in principle but wants rules in place — a December deadline — before any project proceeds. Adds to the wave of small-jurisdiction moratoriums enacted ahead of any state-level Pennsylvania framework.

items.title: Missouri Lawmakers Pass No Data-Center Water/Energy Rules; Local Moratoriums Keep Spreading
items.summary: Missouri's 2026 session ended without advancing HB 3362 (the 'AI Infrastructure Grid Integrity and Water Resources Protection Act'), which would have required a DNR permit for any facility using more than 2 million gallons/day of fresh water and included a drought/grid-emergency kill switch. With no state rule in place, communities are increasingly acting on their own — in Festus, four city council members lost their seats after supporting a $6B data center, and Independence councilmembers were voted out after backing a data-center tax break.

items.title: Most Texas Data Centers Ignore State Water-Use Survey
items.summary: Fewer than a third of Texas's 341 data centers responded to a Public Utility Commission survey on water use — only 28 companies covering 92 facilities answered — prompting lawmakers to call for mandatory disclosure. The non-response rate is the clearest measurement yet of the industry's voluntary-transparency gap in the largest DC growth market.
items.cross_ref_note: Texas groundwater fights tracked in Water Cases tab: Corpus Christi / Sinton — Evangeline Aquifer, TX

items.title: Nvidia Claims AI's Water Challenge Is 'Largely Solved' With Warm-Liquid Cooling
items.summary: At London Climate Week, Nvidia said its newest AI systems can be cooled entirely with liquid warm enough to skip evaporative chilling, 'eliminating pretty much all water usage' in new designs — a supply-side answer to the industry's water problem. Independent verification does not yet exist, and the claim covers new builds, not the installed base.

items.title: Imperial County, CA Declares Emergency Data-Center Moratorium; Developer Sues
items.summary: Imperial County walked back its approval of what would be California's largest data center (1M+ sq ft), declaring a 45-day moratorium and forming a zoning commission; the developer sued for a temporary restraining order, arguing no true emergency exists. A live test of whether emergency land-use powers can pause an already-approved campus.

items.title: Hill County, TX Rescinds Data-Center Moratorium After Federal Lawsuit
items.summary: Facing a federal suit from RCM Hill LLC (developer of the 1,235 MW 'Project Aquila'), Hill County commissioners unanimously rescinded their data-center moratorium; the developer argued no Texas law authorizes a countywide construction pause. Confirms the pattern that Texas counties lack a legal vehicle to slow data-center siting.
items.cross_ref_note: Same no-local-vehicle pattern as MARA bitcoin mine & proposed AI campuses — Hood County, TX in Water Cases tab

items.title: Contentious DEQ Hearing on AWS Lake Anna Cooling-Water Discharge Permit
items.outlet: WWBT 12 On Your Side / Virginia Mercury
items.summary: DEQ's June 9 hearing on the draft VPDES permit letting AWS discharge up to 280,000 gal/day of treated cooling water into a Lake Anna tributary turned combative over chemical additives and the draft's lack of required PFAS testing (DEQ kept only a reopener condition). DEQ says a final permit decision comes after the hearing record closes.
items.cross_ref_note: AWS Lake Anna Technology Campus — Louisa County, VA in Water Cases tab

items.title: More Than Two Dozen North Carolina Communities Restrict Data Centers
items.summary: Over 25 NC communities have adopted moratoriums or zoning restrictions on data centers amid drought-era concerns over water, power, and noise — the densest cluster of local pauses in the country, capped by Charlotte's 150-day citywide moratorium. National context: US data-center water demand could reach 73B gal/yr by 2028, up from ~17B in 2023.
items.cross_ref_note: Charlotte, NC — citywide data-center moratorium in Water Cases tab

items.title: Data-Center Moratorium Bills Introduced in 11 States in 2026
items.summary: State-level moratorium bills have been introduced in 11 states in 2026; most face resistance, while dozens of municipalities move ahead with local construction pauses instead. The state/local split — statewide bills stall, city moratoriums pass — is becoming the defining pattern of the backlash's second year.
items.cross_ref_note: Statewide moratorium bills (e.g. NY S10642 / A11560) in Legislation tab

items.title: UN University: AI Data Centers' 2030 Water Footprint Equals Basic Needs of 1.3B People
items.summary: UN scientists project that by 2030 global AI data centers' water footprint will equal the basic annual domestic water needs of all 1.3 billion people in Sub-Saharan Africa, alongside electricity use tripling the combined consumption of Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Nigeria — the first UN-system quantification of AI's aggregate water draw.

items.title: New York Data Center Bill Passes Legislature, Awaits Hochul Signature
items.summary: The Responsible Data Center Development Act (S10642 / A11560) passed the Senate 44-16 and Assembly 102-39, mandating SEQRA environmental review for any facility exceeding 50 MW. If signed, it would be the broadest state-level environmental review trigger for data centers in the US. Gov. Hochul has not publicly committed as of June 2026.
items.cross_ref_note: NY S10642 / A11560 in Legislation tab

items.title: Bipartisan Michigan Lawmakers Push Data Center Construction Moratorium
items.summary: SB 1018-1020 and companion HB 5594-5596 would impose a moratorium on new data center construction permits until the state completes a water-capacity analysis and Great Lakes Compact review. A bipartisan Capitol event in June renewed pressure, though Senate leadership prefers targeted regulation over a blanket moratorium.
items.cross_ref_note: MI SB 1018-1020 in Legislation tab

items.title: Illinois Governor Pritzker Pauses New Data Center Incentive Agreements
items.summary: After the POWER Act (SB 3830) failed to pass before the session ended, Gov. Pritzker used executive authority to pause new Data Center Investment Program incentive agreements. The move signals growing state reluctance to extend tax incentives without commensurate water and power transparency requirements.
items.cross_ref_note: IL SB 3830 (POWER Act) in Legislation tab

items.title: Google Files §404 Individual Permit Applications for Three Data Center Projects
items.summary: Google filed individual §404 permit applications for Project Raspberry (VA), Project Loch (VA), and a Port of Little Rock (AR) site. The Arkansas application involves 16.8 acres of wetland fill — the largest §404 wetland footprint in any active data center permit. Each application triggers a public comment period and Section 401 water quality certification from the respective state.
items.cross_ref_note: Google §404 permit applications in Water Cases tab: Google ProjectRaspberry VA (2026), Google LittleRock AR (2026)

items.title: Utah Governor Signs Executive Order Requiring Water-Use Review Before Data Center Permits
items.summary: Gov. Spencer Cox signed EO 2026-03 directing state agencies to require water-use impact review before approving large data center projects. The EO also instructs the Department of Natural Resources to evaluate cost-attribution models so developers bear marginal supply expansion costs. It complements Utah HB 76 (enacted March 2026), which mandates projected and actual water disclosure at a 10,000 sq ft threshold.
items.cross_ref_note: UT EO 2026-03 and UT HB 76 in Legislation tab

items.title: Virginia Enacts First Mandatory Data Center Water Reporting Law
items.summary: Gov. Spanberger signed HB 496 (companion SB 553) on April 13, 2026, amending Va. Code § 62.1-44.38 to require water utilities to report monthly aggregate water volumes delivered to data centers. The law is effective July 1, 2026; first published data is expected late 2026. It is the first enacted state law mandating utility-level DC water reporting in the US.
items.cross_ref_note: VA HB 496 / SB 553 in Legislation tab

items.title: Maryland Legislature Overrides Veto to Mandate Data Center Impact Study
items.summary: The Maryland General Assembly voted to override Gov. Moore's veto of HB 270 / SB 116, requiring the Department of Natural Resources to conduct an economic and environmental impact study of large data centers before 2028. The study must include water consumption projections and infrastructure cost allocation.
items.cross_ref_note: MD HB 270 / SB 116 in Legislation tab

items.title: Amazon Pays $20.5M in First Eight-Figure Hyperscaler Water Settlement
items.outlet: Oregon Department of Justice / Oregon DEQ
items.summary: Amazon and its WWTP operator settled with Oregon DEQ and DOJ over nitrogen discharge at the Boardman industrial park — the first direct hyperscaler water-penalty case to reach eight figures. Data center cooling-tower blowdown was among the industrial loads routed to the facility. The settlement funds nutrient trading credits in the Columbia River basin.
items.cross_ref_note: Amazon Boardman OR nitrate (2026) in Water Cases tab — Historical section

items.title: Idaho Becomes First State to Mandate Closed-Loop (Non-Consumptive) Cooling for Data Centers
items.summary: Idaho H895 requires new data center facilities to use closed-loop or non-consumptive cooling systems as a condition of permitting. This eliminates the largest pathway of consumptive water loss — evaporation from open cooling towers. The law is designed to protect groundwater in the Snake River Plain aquifer system.
items.cross_ref_note: ID H 895 in Legislation tab

items.title: South Dakota Enacts 'Data Center Bill of Rights' with Water-Supply Compatibility Rule
items.summary: SB 135 requires data centers ≥10 MW to demonstrate water-supply compatibility before construction approval, and mandates cost-causation billing so developers bear the marginal cost of supply-infrastructure expansions they trigger — not residential ratepayers. Part of a broader 'bill of rights' package addressing grid and water load-shifting.
items.cross_ref_note: SD SB 135 in Legislation tab

items.title: Utah Enacts Water Transparency Amendments Lowering Disclosure Threshold to 10,000 sq ft
items.summary: Utah HB 76 mandates that data centers ≥10,000 sq ft publicly report projected and actual water consumption annually. The 10,000 sq ft threshold was set to align with existing utility metering capabilities. It is a successor to earlier bills that stalled over data-collection infrastructure concerns.
items.cross_ref_note: UT HB 76 in Legislation tab

items.title: California AB 2619 Advances — Successor to Vetoed AB 93
items.summary: AB 2619 (Asm. Papan) advances through committee, requiring data centers to publicly disclose projected and actual water use annually. It is the successor to AB 93, which Gov. Newsom vetoed in October 2024 citing data-collection concerns. Companion SB 887 would add CEQA review requirements. Both bills are expected to see floor votes in summer 2026.
items.cross_ref_note: CA AB 2619 and CA SB 887 in Legislation tab

items.title: Central Ohio Study Projects Data Center Water Demand Growing from 10 to 90 MGD by 2050
items.outlet: Central Ohio Regional Water Authority / Ohio EPA
items.summary: A regional water demand study published March 2025 projects industrial water demand — dominated by planned data center expansions — growing from ~10 MGD today to 40 MGD by 2030 and 90 MGD by 2050. Intel's New Albany campus alone accounts for ~6 MGD. The study is being used to plan $2B+ in regional water infrastructure.
items.cross_ref_note: Central Ohio demand projections in the Data tab

items.title: Ohio EPA Closes Comment Period on First-Ever Data Center Wastewater General Permit
items.summary: Comment period closed January 2025 on Ohio EPA OHD000001 — the first proposed general permit requiring data centers to file Discharge Monitoring Reports (DMRs) directly for cooling-tower blowdown. Currently, most DC cooling water routes through municipal WWTPs with no facility-level accounting. Final permit is still pending.
items.cross_ref_note: OHD000001 in Data tab — Ohio EPA scraper

items.title: UC Riverside 'Making AI Less Thirsty' — First Major Quantification of AI Water Footprint
items.outlet: University of California, Riverside (Shaolei Ren et al.)
items.summary: The landmark study estimated 0.5 L per 10–50 ChatGPT queries (direct cooling only) and up to 500 mL per query when including thermoelectric cooling for electricity generation. It catalyzed policy and media attention on data center water use and established WUE (Water Usage Effectiveness) as a public-facing metric. The viral 'one 500mL bottle per prompt' figure in later coverage was a 50–250× overstatement of this research.
items.cross_ref_note: Per-query estimates discussed in Data tab
